query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing trace amounts of Hf (approximately 0.5–1 at%) into eutectic high‐entropy alloys will form fine Hf-rich precipitates along the internal boundaries of the lamellar microstructure. These precipitates will act to pin and strengthen the interfaces against microcrack initiation and propagation, thereby simultaneously enhancing both the yield strength and room-temperature tensile ductility compared to the unmodified alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies composed of soft and hard phases, possessing numerous internal boundaries that serve as potential sites for microcrack initiation.
generation.intervention: Alloying with a trace amount of Hf (around 0.5–1 at%).
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile deformation with standard thermo-mechanical processing that retains the lamellar colony microstructure; careful control of Hf content to avoid excessive intermetallic formation.
generation.structural_mediator: Fine Hf-rich precipitates that segregate to phase and grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The Hf-rich precipitates reinforce the internal boundaries by serving as barrier pinning points that hinder microcrack nucleation and propagation. Additionally, these precipitates provide precipitation strengthening, collectively leading to an improvement in both strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Hf-modified alloy will display a higher yield strength and enhanced tensile ductility than the baseline eutectic HEA, due to reduced microcrack propagation along the internal boundaries and improved interface cohesion.
generation.baseline: Unmodified eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar structure that suffers from microcrack initiation at internal boundaries, resulting in brittleness and limited tensile ductility at room temperature.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected only with trace Hf additions; if too much Hf is added, the formation of coarse or brittle intermetallic phases may occur, negating the improvements. The hypothesis is primarily applicable to alloys processed to retain a lamellar microstructure under room-temperature tensile loading.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative improvements in strength and ductility and the optimal Hf concentration require further experimental calibration. The interaction of Hf with other alloying elements may also influence the outcome in ways that are not fully predictable.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of eutectic high-entropy alloy samples using the same thermo-mechanical processing: one set with trace Hf additions (0.5–1 at%) and one control set without Hf. Conduct room-temperature tensile tests while using microscopy (e.g., TEM/SEM) to characterize the presence and distribution of Hf-rich precipitates.
measurements: Microstructural analysis of precipitate formation and distribution at internal boundaries
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Hf-modified samples do not demonstrate a simultaneous increase in both yield strength and tensile ductility relative to the control, or if microscopy reveals that Hf leads to deleterious coarse or brittle precipitate formation without beneficial interface pinning, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: As we all know, the alloying of metals with certain specific elements can very effectively improve alloy properties through various strengthening methods such as precipitation strengthening, solution strengthening, and interface strengthening [,,,]. Hf is an essential alloying element for both the interface strengthening of superalloys and the strengthening of the Ni-Al B2 phase [,,,,,]. Recently, some studies have shown that adding a small amount of Hf to a single-phase FCC high-entropy alloy could improve the room-temperature mechanical property of the alloy without significantly reducing the ductility of the alloy through the precipitation of intermetallic compounds such as Ni7Hf2 and Laves phases [,]. However, these studies mainly focus on single-phase high-entropy alloys, and the addition of Hf is relatively large, usually more than one atom. Therefore, the effect of trace Hf addition on the properties of the alloy at room temperature and high temperature is worthy of in-depth investigation.

The strengthening effect of Hf on the alloy could be maintained at 600 °C, 800 °C, and 900 °C.At different high temperatures, the Hf0.5 alloy exhibited a higher strength and ductility than the Hf0 alloys. The outstanding high-temperature strength of the Hf0.5 alloy was attributed to the precipitation strengthening of the Hf-rich phase precipitated in the inner of the B2 phase. The excellent high-temperature ductility of the Hf0.5 alloy was attributed to the pinning effect of the Hf-rich phase that existed at grain and phase boundaries to boundary sliding during the high-temperature deformation.
